transcript.text: Our Bosch dryer keeps stopping with the empty water container light on but the container is empty?? We've emptied it like 5 times

That's a frustrating one, but it's very common on Bosch condenser and heat pump dryers. The light usually isn't reading the container itself. It's triggered by a float switch in a sump at the bottom of the machine. If water can't get from the sump up to the container, the sump fills, the float rises, and the dryer stops, even though the container is empty.

Here's what to check, roughly in order of likelihood:

1. Reset properly after emptying
• Push the container all the way in until it clicks and sits flush. If it's slightly out, the light can stay on.
• Some models need you to press Start/Pause again, or turn the dryer off and on, to clear the light.

2. Is the dryer plumbed into a drain?
If a hose runs from the back of the dryer to a sink or standpipe:
• Check the hose for kinks, especially if the dryer was moved recently.
• Make sure the hose end isn't pushed too far down the drain or sitting in water.
• Check the drain itself isn't blocked.

3. Clean the filters
• Door fluff filter: clean it every load.
• Heat exchanger / condenser (usually behind a panel at the bottom front): heavy lint build-up here often clogs the pump.
• On heat pump models, there's often a sponge or foam filter in that bottom compartment. Rinse it under the tap until it's clean, and let it dry or squeeze it out before refitting.
• Some models also have a small filter inside the water container itself. Rinse that too.

4. Clear the pump inlet / sump
With the condenser or heat exchanger removed, look in the cavity it sits in. Lint and gunk collect there and block the pump. Wipe it out, and check the rubber seals are clean.

5. Drain the sump
Unplug the dryer first. Then tilt it back slightly over a towel or tray. Sometimes water sitting in the sump keeps the float raised, and draining it lets the float reset.

6. Check for a stuck float
If water is still in the sump after the above, the float may be stuck with lint. Gently tilting or rocking the machine can free it.

If none of that works
The condensate pump has probably failed or is jammed. A classic sign is that you hear a humming but no gurgling or pumping. This is a fairly cheap part, and a competent DIYer or a technician can replace it.

If you tell me the model number, I can point you more precisely to where the filters are. It's usually on a sticker inside the door rim, starting with "WTG", "WTH", "WTW" or similar.

Container clicks in fine, and there's no drain hose, it just uses the container. I've cleaned the container's little filter (it was slimy) and the fluff and condenser filters, which were fairly clean. I can't tilt or drain it though, it's stacked on the washing machine with a tower kit. The manual says it starts WTG8 but the full label is on the back, which I can't get to.

Good that you've ruled those out. The slimy container filter is a useful clue: that same gunk has probably built up further back in the system, in the pump or the pipe that carries water up to the container.

Finding the model number without moving it
On most Bosch dryers the rating plate is also inside the door opening, on the rim of the frame. Look for an E-Nr (e.g. WTG86400GB/01) and an FD number. That gives you the exact model for parts, diagrams, or booking a repair. Most WTG8 models are condenser dryers, not heat pump.

Things you can still do while it's stacked

1. Clean the condenser cavity properly
   With the condenser out, shine a torch into the space it sits in. Look for lint, slime, or standing water at the bottom, and around the openings and seals at the back. Mop out any water with a sponge or old cloth, or use a wet/dry vacuum if you have one. The pump sits just below this area, so gunk here often blocks it.

2. Check the container's housing
   Pull the container out and look into the slot it sits in, especially the small inlet where water drips in. If the slime from the filter has dried around there, wipe it clean.

3. Do a quick pump test
   Empty the container, then run a short drying cycle on a damp load for 15 to 20 minutes.
   • Water appears in the container: the pump is working, and the fault is more likely the float switch or its sensor.
   • No water at all, and the light comes on again: the pump is blocked or has failed, or the pipe to the container is clogged.
   You may also hear the pump running as a short buzz or whirr every so often. Silence suggests it isn't working.

If it still stops
The remaining fixes, like clearing the pump, freeing a stuck float, or replacing the pump, mean getting into the base of the machine. That needs the dryer unstacked. Don't try tilting it while it's on the tower kit, as it could come off the bracket. If you're happy doing it yourself, unstack it with two people and drain the sump. Otherwise, this is a reasonable job to book with Bosch or a local appliance engineer, and the E-Nr and FD numbers will help them bring the right parts. Pump replacements on these models are common and not usually a big job.

To stop it happening again
Rinse the container filter and wipe out the condenser cavity every few weeks. Slime building up is often the start of this problem.

I found a small cover down by the condenser and behind it was grey slimy water and fluff, so I wiped out what I could reach. It then ran for about an hour instead of 20-40 minutes, but the light came on again. I couldn't tell you if the pump buzzes, as I don't know what I'm listening for. I haven't looked for a label inside the door rim, so I'm not sure it's there.

That's real progress. Running for an hour instead of 20 to 40 minutes means you cleared part of the blockage, but something is still restricting the water. The pump, the pipe up to the container, or the float is probably still partly gummed up.

One key question: after that hour-long run, was there any water in the container?
• Some water: the pump works but is struggling, likely partial blockage. More cleaning may fix it.
• Bone dry: water isn't getting up to the container at all. The pump or pipe is blocked, or the pump is failing.

Have another go at that cover area
That's the right spot. It's the sump, where the pump and float sit.
• Soak up as much of the standing water as you can with a sponge or cloth. Leftover water keeps the float raised.
• Use a bottle brush, old toothbrush, or cotton buds to get into corners and around any openings you can see. Fluff tends to wrap around the pump inlet.
• Wipe the cover's seal and the lip it sits on.

A test to hear the pump
1. Empty the container and start a drying cycle.
2. After a few minutes, slowly pour a cupful of water into the condenser cavity, near that cover.
3. Listen and watch. A working pump makes a short whirr or hum for a few seconds, often with a gurgle, and water should trickle into the container soon after.

This tells you whether the pump is working and shows you what to listen for. Pour slowly, and don't use more than a cup or two.

Finding the model label
With the door open, look around the rim of the opening, especially the top or sides, and on the inside edge of the door itself. It's a small sticker with "E-Nr" and "FD." If it isn't there, it's only on the back.

If it still stops
If the cup test shows no water reaching the container, or the light keeps coming back after a thorough clean, the remaining fix is inside the base. The pump or pipe needs clearing, or the pump needs replacing. That means unstacking it with two people, or calling Bosch or a local appliance repairer. The model number will help either way.

Not sure about the water, I didn't look closely, but the container looked nearly empty when the light came on. I'm not really confident about pouring water into the dryer to test the pump. Can you tell me exactly where I'd pour it, or is there something safer to try first?

That's sensible caution. There's a safer test to try first, and if you do try the water test, it can be done with the dryer unplugged.

"Nearly empty" is already a clue. A normal load produces a fair bit of water, often half a litre or more. So if the container had almost nothing after an hour, very little water is getting up to it.

## Safer first: a watched test run (no pouring)

1. Empty the container and refit it.
2. Put in 3 or 4 damp towels. Spin them in the washer first so they're damp, not dripping.
3. Start a normal drying cycle.
4. Every 10 to 15 minutes, pull the container out briefly and look inside. (Pause the dryer first if your model complains when you open it.)
5. Listen while it runs. The pump sounds like a short hum or buzz lasting a few seconds, a bit like a fridge kicking in or a small fish-tank pump, often followed by a gurgle or trickle. You'd expect it every few minutes once water starts building up.

What it tells you:
• Water steadily collecting and you hear the hum: the pump works but is partly blocked. More cleaning of the sump area may fix it.
• Little or no water, no hum, and the light comes on: the pump or the pipe to the container is blocked, or the pump has failed.

## If you want to try the water test: do it with the power off

The water from drying normally drains into that exact area anyway, so a small amount poured there is what the machine is designed to handle. Here's the safer way:

1. Turn the dryer off and unplug it.
2. Open the bottom flap and remove the condenser, as you did for cleaning.
3. Take off the small cover where you found the grey water.
4. Slowly pour about half a cup of water into the cavity behind that cover, where the dirty water was sitting. Don't pour anywhere else, and don't overfill. Stop if it starts pooling up toward the edge.
5. Refit the cover, put the condenser back, and close the flap properly.
6. Plug in, empty the container, and start a cycle.
7. Within a minute or two you should hear the pump hum and see water appear in the container.

If nothing happens and the light comes on quickly, the pump or pipe is blocked or the pump has failed.

## After that

If either test shows little or no water reaching the container, you've done what you can from the front. The rest means getting into the base, so it needs unstacking (two people) or a repairer. It's worth checking the door rim for that E-Nr label before you call, so they can bring the right pump if needed.
